catalog_quote: Тональная система Д.я. трехуровневая. Выделяются высокий (á), средний (ā) и низкий (à) тоны: má ‛кто?’, mā ‛мама’, mà ‛этот’. Тоны в Д.я., помимо лексических, имеют грамматические функции, в первую очередь — маркирование видовременных конструкций. Глагол в конструкции будущего времени получает грамматический низкий тон, при этом предикативный показатель несет высокий тон. Тональные изменения также претерпевают глаголы при образовании их перфективных и имперфективных форм. Автоматические контекстные изменения имеют место только при взаимодействии находящихся по соседству высоких (В) и низких (Н) тонов. В частности, последовательность ННВ заменяется на НВН: bàà ‛козел’ fàlá ‛два’ — bàà fálà. Тональная система Д.я. нуждается в дальнейшем изучении. 5.1.1. Слог может иметь вид V и CV. Слоги в Д.я. преимущественно открытые, закрытые слоги встречаются только в экспрессивных наречиях и в заимствованиях. [Vydrin, family overview, p. 34:] У д а р е н и е в большинстве М.я. отсутствует. Там, где оно может быть выделено (в частности, бамана), его функциональная нагрузка невелика.

new_statements.translation: The tonal system of Jogo is three-level. High (á), mid (ā) and low (à) tones are distinguished: má 'who?', mā 'mother', mà 'this'. Besides lexical functions, tones in Jogo have grammatical functions, primarily the marking of TAM constructions. [...] Automatic contextual changes take place only in the interaction of adjacent high (H) and low (L) tones; in particular the sequence LLH is replaced by LHL: bàà 'goat' fàlá 'two' -> bàà fálà. [...] 5.1.1. The syllable may have the shape V and CV. (Nothing is said about stress; the family overview in the same volume, Vydrin p. 34, states: 'Stress is absent in most Mande languages. Where it can be identified (notably Bamana), its functional load is small.')

new_statements.rule_in_words: Jogo (the Soko variety of the Ligbi/Numu cluster) is described as a tone language with three level tones (H, M, L) carrying lexical and grammatical load; the sketch's prosody section mentions no word stress or accent at all, and the family overview in the same volume says stress is absent in most Mande languages. No source that was opened states a stress position for Ligbi.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress; tonal sandhi LLH -> LHL noted; plural marker no copies the tone of the preceding foot.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level lexical tone with grammatical tone on verbs/predicative markers; the description is of the Soko (Cote d'Ivoire) Jogo idiom, not Ghanaian Ligbi proper.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted sketch (Sapozhnikova 2017) describes Jogo (self-name jɔ́gɔ́, 'Numu') as spoken in Soko village, Bondoukou dept., Cote d'Ivoire, and explicitly says Jogo and the Ligbi of Soko 'are considered different languages'; Glottolog 5.x nevertheless files this article under Ligbi ligb1244 (Jogo-Jeri > Jogo > Ligbi), and ISO lig covers both the Ghana (Banda, Menji, Namasa, Brohani) and Bondoukou-area speakers. Williams 2018 (not obtained) describes the Jogo dialect of Ligbi at Banda/Menji, Ghana, i.e. Ligbi proper. Any catalog entry from Sapozhnikova should be flagged 'Jogo of Soko (CI) variety'.

new_statements.quote: According to Persson and Persson (1980a, b), quoted by Dakubu (1988:161), the tonal system of Jogo has two contrastive level tones, High and Low. [...] Although tone will not be discussed in this study, it has been observed or discovered that Jogo is a contour language - with a rising tone, to be treated in subsequent publication. [...] (7) a. kǔ ‘corps’, b. kǎ ‘snake’, c. bǔ ‘faeces’, d. kʊ̃̌ ‘testicles’, e. sã̌ ‘chief’ With the exception of the H and L tone which bring some lexical difference in meaning, as wùlú ‘dog’, and wúlú ‘lorry/vehicle’ among others, none, including the contour tone, brings a grammatical change to a sentence or phrase.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog's type (classification tonal, no stress rule; Sapozhnikova 2017 read as 'tone language, no stress statement'): Williams likewise treats Jogo as tonal and makes no statement about word stress. It differs from Sapozhnikova on the tone inventory (Williams: 2 level tones H/L + rising contour, citing Persson & Persson 1980/Dakubu 1988 and his own observation; Sapozhnikova: three levels H/M/L, e.g. má/mā/mà) and on grammatical tone (Williams p. 21: tones bring no grammatical change; Sapozhnikova: tone marks TAM constructions). These are tone-analysis differences, not a stress conflict; Williams did not analyse tone ('tone will not be discussed in this study').
new_statements.rule_in_words: Jogo is described as a tone language: two contrastive level tones (High, Low, after Persson & Persson 1980 via Dakubu 1988) plus a rising (LH) contour tone the author reports on monosyllables; tone is lexically contrastive (wùlú 'dog' vs wúlú 'lorry'); tone is explicitly excluded from the thesis's analysis. Nothing is said about word stress or accent in Jogo: the thesis has no stress/accent/prosody section; the only occurrences of 'stress' are in P-Rule 2 (/t/ -> [th] / #__[+stress], '[th] occurs at the onset of a stressed syllable', printed p. 37 = PDF p. 59, repeated App. D printed p. 108 = PDF p. 130), which illustrates levels of representation with the ENGLISH word 'tell', not Jogo; 'accent' elsewhere means tone diacritics or dialectal accent.
new_statements.secondary_stress: none mentioned (no stress statement at all)
new_statements.exceptions: none regarding stress; on tone: the author says the contour (rising) tone, unlike H vs L, carries no lexical or grammatical contrast he observed
new_statements.identity_note: Williams describes Jogo as spoken by the Ligbi of Banda (Brong-Ahafo Region, Ghana), i.e. Ligbi ligb1244; the Numu variety of Brohani ('Ton/Tonjon/Ntɔgɔlɛ') is mentioned only in the dialect survey (sec. 1.2.2.2) and is not analysed.
